steps.prompt: There are $10$ stones. You and a friend take turns removing $1$ or $2$. Whoever takes the last stone wins. Would you rather go first or second?

cards.title: Winning and losing positions
cards.body: Work backwards from the end. A position is LOSING if every move leads to a winning position for the other player, and WINNING if some move leads to a losing one. With "take $1$ to $k$, last stone wins", the losing piles are the multiples of $k + 1$.

cards.title: Worked example: ten stones
cards.problem: In the hook game (take $1$ or $2$, last stone wins), how many should the first player take from $10$?

steps.text: The losing piles are multiples of $3$: $0, 3, 6, 9$.

try.prompt: Which losing pile can you leave from $10$?

steps.text: So take $1$, then always make $3$ with your opponent.

cards.title: Symmetry and counting
cards.body: Copy your opponent: equal piles in two-pile Nim, or the mirror move on a symmetric board. Some "games" have a fixed answer: every break of a chocolate bar adds one piece, and every match in a knockout removes one player.

cards.title: Worked example: a knockout
cards.problem: $20$ players enter a knockout tournament. How many matches are played?

steps.text: Each match knocks out exactly one player.

try.prompt: How many players must be knocked out?

steps.text: So $19$ matches, however the rounds are arranged.

cards.title: The common trap: thinking forwards
cards.body: Don't play the game forwards from the start. Start from the end, find the losing positions, and spot their pattern. Check: is the safe step $k + 1$ (not $k$)?

prompts: How do you find the losing positions of a game?
